Filling the Void: How Competing Brands Can Capitalize on a Brand Deletion

ABSTRACT

Brand manufacturers, big and small, regularly prune their brand portfolios by deleting

their brands from categories. Competing brands try to fill the void, with potentially varying

consequences for sister brands by the same manufacturer, rival national brands, and private

labels. As little is known about these consequences, this research analyzes systematically

whether these three brand types benefit and how they adjust their marketing conduct following a

brand deletion. Using a difference-in-differences analysis of 1,046 FMCG national brand

deletions observed over 10 years affecting competing brands sold across 201 US markets and 55

retailers (with about 63,000 market-retailer-category-brand combinations affected), the findings

reveal that the outcomes of the deletions are strongly shaped by how brands adjust their

marketing mix after the brand deletion. By lifting distribution (which is highly effective), private

labels are the largest beneficiaries of brand deletions, followed by sister brands (successfully

lifting line length), and, lastly, rival national brands. There are also lost opportunities (little

change in price promotion across brand types, spoiled arms (hike in ineffective feature

advertising), and self-inflicted losses (regular price hikes that decrease revenue). Manufacturers

retain only 38% of the deleted brand’s revenue through sister brands on average, showing the

risk of brand pruning.

Keywords: Marketing Mix, Brand Management, Marketing Strategy

Page 3

Brand manufacturers, big and small, regularly engage in pruning by deleting brands from

categories. In their efforts to manage their extensive brand portfolios across many product

categories, often with multiple brands within the same category, P&G announced in 2014 plans

to shrink its brand portfolio by more than half by retiring as many as 100 brands (Wall Street

Journal 2014). Coca-Cola indicated it will discontinue 200 brands, including its Tab, Zico, and

Odwalla beverage brands (Wall Street Journal 2020). Not just global conglomerates, but also

smaller brand manufacturers frequently delete brands from their portfolios. Brand manufacturers

mention a variety of reasons for brand deletions, ranging from brands underperforming or having

low growth potential (Crespo 2018), brand portfolio simplification and increased efficiencies

(Morning Brew 2020), reducing overlap in targeted customer segments (Rose 2025), to changing

consumer preferences resulting in shrinking categories (Unilever 2025).

Such deletions offer several strategic benefits, including cost savings (e.g., in procurement,

production, inventory, distribution, salespeople, and opportunity costs), greater efficiency, and a

sharper focus on core brands. In addition, brand manufacturers hope that some customers of the

deleted brand will simply switch to “sister brands” within the same manufacturer’s portfolio

(Kumar 2003), if such sister brands exist. However, the extent to which these sister brands (if

available) actually benefit from deletions has not been documented though, or what the effects

might be for other brands in the market, such as rival national brands (owned by other

manufacturers) and, if available, private labels (owned by retailers). It is also not clear what

manufacturers of the different brands can do to reap these benefits.

Arguably, one brand’s demise could benefit other brands in the product category, which

may capture the deleted brand’s business. Thus, we study changes in the marketing conduct of

sister brands, rival national brands, and private labels following a focal brand’s exit from a

Page 4

product category. In the context of FMCG (our research context), marketing conduct includes

manufacturer-driven decisions (feature advertising and price promotion), retailer decisions with

manufacturers’ input (regular price and line length, i.e., the number of SKUs that a brand

carries), and retailer-driven decisions (distribution).1 Competing brands may strengthen their

marketing support to seize the opportunity offered by the deleted brand’s exit, or weaken it

because competition has been softened. Both changes can be considered as responses to the

brand deletion, as long as they involve statistically significant changes in competing brand

marketing conduct when a brand is deleted compared to the case where it is not deleted.

While extant marketing literature offers plenty of guidance for new brand launches, there is

very little consideration of how competing brands might fill voids left behind by another brand’s

permanent deletion from all retailers. Although the literature has focused on temporary SKU

removals (e.g., Campo, Gijsbrechts, and Nisol 2000; Campo, Gijsbrechts, and Nisol 2003;

Campo, Gijsbrechts, and Nisol 2004; Sloot, Fok, and Verhoef 2006) and permanent SKU

deletions (e.g., Boatwright and Nunes 2001; Broniarczyk, Hoyer, and McAlister 1998; Sloot et

al. 2006), research has not studied deletions where a brand is deleted at all retailers. Instead,

other papers have looked at the implications of temporary out-of-stock situations (Verbeke,

Farris, and Thurik 1998), conflict delistings (Van der Maelen, Breugelmans, and Cleeren 2017),

and the deletion of a brand at one but not at all retailers (Sloot and Verhoef 2008).

To the best of our knowledge though, no research has dealt with permanent brand deletions

from a product category across all retailers, which constitute a deliberate strategic decision to

withdraw the brand permanently from the product category and from all retailers in a market. As

such, permanent brand deletions differ fundamentally from (1) out-of-stock situations, which are

1 In other contexts (e.g., digital marketing), marketing conduct includes other marketing activities, e.g., through social media, banner ads, or email.

Page 5

not deliberate and not permanent; (2) conflict deletions, which do not apply to the entire market

and are not permanent, (3) SKU deletions, which are tactical decisions, (4) adoption of an

exclusive distribution strategy, where the brand is only sold at select retailers, and (5) the

deletion of a brand at one but not at all retailers.

In making strategic brand deletion decisions, all SKUs of a brand disappear from a

category across all retailers, making these decisions highly noticeable and relevant to consumers

and competitors. To understand the performance implications of brand deletions, we need

empirical insights into which remaining brands benefit. If sister brands benefit exclusively, it

supports brand pruning for the manufacturer, as revenues shift within the portfolio rather than

being lost. However, if rival national brands benefit and little goes to sister brands, the

manufacturer of the deleted brand may regret its brand-pruning strategy. Finally, if private labels

benefit, the brand deletion shifts more power to retailers. As these hypothetical outcomes imply,

assessing which brand benefits the most from brand deletions has crucial ramifications for the

manufacturer, its rivals, and its retailer partners.

We also need to consider if and how brands may leverage their marketing mix to ensure

that redistributed demand comes to them. For example, a brand could offer price promotions, use

feature advertising, expand its product line, increase distribution, and/or adjust its regular price.

Rival national brands may undertake such marketing efforts in the wake of the brand deletion,

but so could sister brands from the same manufacturer, aiming to keep demand “in the family.”

Retailers may also see an opportunity to capitalize on the deleted brand’s demise by pushing

their own private labels. Thus far, “little is known about how marketing mix actions … can be

used to mitigate the negative consequences of product unavailability” (Breugelmans, Gijsbrechts,

and Campo 2018, p. 217). Understanding how such marketing efforts affect redistribution

Page 6

outcomes is crucial for designing an informed response to a brand deletion from a category.

To document what happens in the wake of a brand deletion, this paper addresses four

pertinent research questions. First, when a brand leaves the category, which competing brand

type gains the most in terms of revenue: sister national brands, rival national brands, or private

labels, and how is category revenue affected? Second, how are these gains moderated by the

characteristics of the deleted brand (e.g., pre-deletion market share), the competing brand (e.g.,

similarity in price positioning to deleted brand), or the category (e.g., concentration)? Third, to

what extent do competing brands change their marketing conduct significantly in the wake of the

brand deletion? Fourth, how do competing brands fare overall after the brand deletion, taking

into account the extent to which they engage in marketing mix adjustments?

To address these questions, we adopt an empirics-first (EF) approach (Golder et al. 2023)

rather than a theory-first approach because little theory predicts post-deletion outcomes. We

document empirical regularities, using U.S. scanner data over 10 years with 1,046 national brand

deletions, from 201 designated market areas (DMAs), and within the top 3 retailers in each

market. The deletions affect 6,031 brands competing in the same categories, resulting in over

63,000 market-retailer-category-brand combinations.

We use a stacked difference-in-differences approach with “not-yet-treated” cases as

control units, combined with instrumental variables to account for potential endogeneity in the

brand deletion timing and marketing mix. Using this setup, we find that a brand deletion benefits

competing brands, increasing their sales by 1.73% on average. But not all brands benefit equally:

retailers’ private labels benefit the most (+3.45% revenue), followed by sister brands (+2.77%)

and rival national brands (+1.36%). Competing brands gain more revenue when they have

greater price similarity with the deleted brand, when the deleted brand’s pre-deletion market

Page 7

share is higher, and when the category is less concentrated. A large part of these revenue gains is

attributable to marketing mix adjustments. All brand types manage to increase their distribution

in the wake of the brand deletion, which, when combined with strong distribution elasticities,

leads to revenue gains of 1.23%-1.77%. One surprising result is that only sister brands increase

their line length in the wake of the brand deletion, which (combined with a strong line length

elasticity) generates an additional .84% revenue gain. We also find evidence for lost

opportunities in marketing conduct (hardly any change in the use of very effective price

promotion), self-inflicted losses (regular price hikes even though this hurts brand revenue), and

spoiled arms (lift in relatively ineffective feature advertising compared to the control group). We

also find that on average, manufacturers retain only about 38% of the deleted brand’s sales, with

strong variation in this percentage across cases.

RELATED LITERATURE

A stream of prior literature focuses on what happens when a product, SKU, or brand is

temporarily delisted or permanently deleted. As Table 1 shows, most of these studies focus on

cases where the brand remains available but specific SKUs are temporarily delisted or

permanently deleted.

Temporary brand delistings have been studied in the context of manufacturer–retailer

conflicts and stockouts. For example, Van der Maelen et al. (2017) demonstrate that both

manufacturers and retailers experience sales losses during conflict delistings. Although retailers

are hit harder during the delisting period, they often recover, while manufacturers emerge

stronger and enjoy higher post-delisting sales. In contrast, Hermans, Raassens, and Cleeren

(2024) document severe negative effects of conflict delistings on the stock market value of both

manufacturers and retailers. They also show how the effectiveness of advertising and price

Page 8

promotions varies with conflict characteristics such as elimination size, publicity, and initiator.

Vafainia et al. (2025) take a broader view of conflict delistings by studying not only involved

brands and categories, but also uninvolved brands, categories, and even uninvolved retailers, and

how price and promotion adjustments can shape these temporary cross-category spillover effects.

Rather than temporary brand deletions that are typically restricted to just one retailer, we

study permanent brand deletions across all retailers. Since our focal brand deletions occur across

all retailers, the deletion is more of a manufacturer’s decision than a decision by a specific

Page 9

retailer. Retailers and manufacturers tend to be rather silent on permanent brand deletions, which

is different from conflict delistings that are widely discussed in the (business) press and can be

observed in-store by customers through the empty shelves with notifications about the delistings.

Our study also differs from Sloot and Verhoef (2008, SV2008 from now on) studying the

case where a brand disappears permanently at some but not all retailers, which allows customers

to find the brand elsewhere. SV2008 uses an online lab experiment and a survey to study the

impact of brand deletions on store and brand switching intentions, moderated by the deleted

brand’s characteristics and category characteristics. Our study extends SV2008 by studying

brand deletions across all retailers (not just at one retailer) and by going beyond intentions and

measuring the revenue effects of brand deletions for competing brands and the category.

Another point of difference is that SV2008 does not measure which competing brands

benefit from the brand deletion, nor how these brands change their marketing conduct. What our

paper adds to the literature is that we study which types of competing brands (rival national

brands, sister brands, private labels) gain from the brand deletion, what moderates these gains,

how marketing conduct changes in the wake of the brand deletion, and how competing brands

fare overall after the brand deletion, taking into account their marketing conduct.

STUDY FRAMEWORK

We present the study framework in Figure 1. We purposefully refrain from directional

hypotheses but include the figure to help visualize the focal relationships, labelled (A)-(D).

Specifically, Figure 1 depicts the brand deletion as the focal event, with potential revenue gains

for rival national brands, sister brands, and private labels (A). The literature on brand switching

offers insights into which type of brands may benefit most. Since national brands compete more

with other national brands rather than private labels (e.g., Blattberg and Wisniewski 1989), we

Page 10

may expect rival national brands and sister brands to benefit the most. We also examine how

brand deletion affects category revenue, which may be negative (if the deleted brand’s demand is

not fully absorbed by competing brands), neutral (if others gain as much as is lost), or positive (if

competing brands expand the category).

Next, we study moderators shaping these gains (B in Figure 1). In particular, the larger

the deleted brand (as indicated by its market share), the greater the potential gains for

competitors (Sloot and Verhoef 2008). The competing brand’s market share may also influence

gains, positively if larger brands have more pull, or negatively due to ceiling effects (Fok and

Franses 2004). Competing brands may be better positioned to grow revenue if their price

positioning aligns more closely with that of the deleted brand (Blattberg and Wisniewski 1989).

The other two moderators are category growth (which should lift the gain as the pie is growing)

and category concentration (which may reduce the gain as it may be harder to find a suitable

substitute in a category with a few big brands).

Figure 1. Study Framework

Notes: Sister brands refer to brands owned by the same manufacturer as that of the deleted brand, rival national brands refer to brands owned by other manufacturers, and private labels refer to retailer-owned brands.

Page 11

Each competing brand can adjust its marketing conduct (captured by promotion price,

feature advertising, regular price, line length, and distribution in our FMCG context2) to steer

more revenue its way after a brand deletion (C in Figure 1). The direction of change can go either

way. When the focal brand is deleted, competition softens, and competing brands may reduce

marketing support (fewer price promotions or features, higher regular price, shorter line length,

and less distribution). Conversely, the deleted brand’s exit leaves a gap that competitors may

seek to fill by increasing their marketing support. Finally, we explore how the same moderators

shape these changes in competing brands’ marketing conduct after a brand deletion (D in Figure

1). For instance, depending on the deleted brand’s market share or the category concentration,

competing brands may respond more aggressively in adjusting their marketing conduct.

DATA AND MEASURES Deleted Brands

For a broad investigation of what happens in the wake of a brand deletion, we focus on

all national brand deletions across all FMCG categories across a ten-year time period (2010–

2019) from any brand manufacturer, ranging from small to large. We hence do not consider

private label deletions. We identify brand deletions based on RMS NielsenIQ scanner data at the

market-retailer-category-brand-week level. These scanner data cover more than 1,300 product

categories in nine departments, such as health and beauty aids, food and beverages, dairy, and

non-food grocery products. We adopt the NielsenIQ definitions of categories, and give a

complete list of categories in our sample in Web Appendix A. We assume that all brands within a

category can be alternatives to the deleted brand, and if they are not, this will show up

empirically as null effects. As our focus is on brand deletions (rather than sub-brand deletions,

2 Brands often carry a narrower range of products at a specific retailer in a specific market than across all retailers and markets in the country. Thus, it is relatively easy for them to extend their line length at a specific retailer on short notice.

Page 12

which is more similar to previously-studied product line deletions), we aggregate NielsenIQ’s

sub-brands (e.g., “Air Wick Double Fresh”, “Air Wick Essential Mist”, “Air Wick Fresh Matic”,

and “Air Wick Hidden Pleasures”) to the brand level (“Air Wick”). We decide to keep the

NielsenIQ definitions of categories because they cater to different segments and have their own

price levels (and at times different measurement units) and differentiated marketing activities.

We screen all product categories and identify deletions from any category for any

national brand. We define a brand as deleted if it disappears from a product category and is

eventually deleted across all markets (DMAs) in the U.S and does not reappear for at least one

year. To ensure sufficient economic substance, we focus on deleted brands with (i) at least 52

weeks of observations, (ii) at least $10k in revenue across the U.S. in the year prior to the

deletion, and (iii) at least $100 in weekly sales at a given retailer and market before the deletion.

Thus, we identify 1,046 deleted national brands and show a selection in Table 2. Figure 2

provides an overview of the distribution of the deleted brands’ market shares prior to the

beginning of the deletion.

Brand deletions typically are not executed simultaneously across the entire U.S. at once

but rather occur sequentially, separately by markets (DMAs) and within markets, by retailers. We

account for the role of retailers as gatekeepers by analyzing brand deletions at the market-

retailer-brand level (14,462 market-retailer-deleted brand combinations). This allows us to

include retailer-specific marketing mix adjustments and retailer-specific moderators of the

treatment effect.

Within each market and retailer, a brand deletion is not an instantaneous event. A brand

deletion begins with a drop in its distribution (T0) and ends when the brand is no longer

distributed (T1). Distribution is the weighted average of the percentage of stores that carry the

Page 14

brand, where the weight is the store’s total annual revenue (all commodity value; Farris, Olver,

and De Kluyver 1989). To assess the beginning of the deletion, we smooth the distribution using

a moving average over 13 weeks. We then define T0 (beginning of the deletion) as the earlier of

either the last increase in distribution (i.e., no subsequent increase) before the downward slide

begins (98% of cases) or a cumulative drop in distribution that reaches at least 20% without

recovery to the previous distribution level (2% of cases).

Figure 3 depicts brand deletions for a simulated sample case: Talenti pulling out of the

frozen novelties category in one market at one retailer. Here, the beginning of the deletion period

is determined using the last increase in distribution prior to a downward slide. Figure W1 in Web

Appendix B shows the distribution of brand deletion periods across all brand deletions at the

market-retailer level in our sample. The average brand deletion period is 22 weeks, while more

than 30% are deleted within one week, and almost 90% within one year.

Competing Brands

Our analysis focuses on how a brand deletion affects competing brands at the level of

individual retailers within markets. We study all market-retailer-category-brand deletion

combinations with a deletion period of up to 104 weeks at the market-retailer-category level. For

a clean analysis, we require no overlapping brand deletions in the same category in the deletion

period; if that is the case, the quasi-experiment is discarded. To ensure enough economic

substance, we include, for each market where the brand deletion happens, the market’s top 10

competing brands (i.e., rival national brands, sister brands, and private labels) with at least $100

revenue per week, market, and retailer on average, and the market’s top 3 retailers. We study all

available combinations of these top 10 brands at the top 3 retailers, noting that not every brand is

sold at every retailer. To ensure enough observations for inferences, we require at least 52 weeks

of sales data before and after the brand deletion (cf. Cleeren, van Heerde, and Dekimpe 2013).

Each competing brand may be a sister brand, which is a national brand owned by the

same brand manufacturer, a rival national brand owned by another brand manufacturer, or a

private label owned by the retailer. In total, we observe 6,031 unique competing brands,

potentially affected by the 1,046 brand deletions across markets and retailers.3 As our focal unit

of analysis, we use market-retailer-category-brand combinations, reflecting the combination of a

3 Across markets and retailers, we observe 14,462 market-retailer-category-deleted brand combinations. In 95% (= 13,723/14,462), a rival national brand is present, in 57% (=8,275/14,462) a private label, and in 19% (=2,769/14,462) a sister brand.

Page 16

competing brand at a retailer within a market that potentially benefits from a brand deletion from

that same market and retailer. Our analysis includes competitor marketing mix variables to

account for changes in their marketing conduct prior to, during, and after the brand deletion. As

importantly, these variables can be actively adjusted: for instance, manufacturer-driven decisions

such as price promotions and feature advertising have frequently been shown to shift in response

to competitive shifts. Also, retailer decisions with manufacturers’ input, such as regular price and

line length, can be altered; the latter by launching SKUs that already exist in other markets. Even

a retailer-driven decision, such as distribution, though often high, is rarely 100% across all stores

in a market (not even for private labels), leaving scope for further adjustment. We note that a

retailer has, on average, 21.21 stores in a specific market.

To illustrate what market-retailer-category-brand pairs look like, let us consider the brand

deletion by Talenti from the frozen novelties category in a simulated market at one retailer

(Figure 2). Talenti is manufactured by Unilever, and the three sister brands available in the

simulated market are Magnum, Klondike, and Popsicle. The six rival national brands are Blue

Bunny, Dreyer’s, Häagen-Dazs, M&M, Nestle, and The Skinny Cow, and there is one private

label. Therefore, this brand deletion potentially affects 10 competing brands.

METHOD

To estimate the effect of a brand deletion on competing brand revenue and marketing

activity, our analysis proceeds as follows. We leverage a before–after–with–control setting to

estimate the treatment effect of a brand deletion on competing brands, at the market-retailer-

category-competing brand level (63,037 combinations). We use a difference-in-differences model

applied to data at the market (m)-retailer (r)-category (c)-competing brand (b)-week (t) level. The

model is augmented with moderators of the treatment effect and marketing mix effects. We also

estimate difference-in-differences models for the levels of the marketing mix variables of

competing brands, to assess how much they engage in marketing conduct changes.

We now discuss some identification challenges for estimating treatment effects and how

we address them. First, competing brands’ sales can change over time, even without the brand

deletion. To account for this possibility, we use as a control the same competing brand at the

same retailer in other markets. This approach accounts for seasonal effects and trends that affect

both the treated and control units. The fact that we observe “staggered treatment timing” for each

brand deletion and expect heterogeneous treatment effects requires special care because the

standard two-way fixed effects estimator may be biased (Goodman-Bacon 2021). We deal with

this as follows: we identify for each “treated” case (a market-retailer-category-deleted brand-

competing brand combination) a set of control units that consist of “not-yet-treated” cases. That

is, these “not-yet-treated” cases are not treated while they serve as a control unit, i.e., at least

until one year after the end of the post-deletion period, and as such, they present clean control

cases. We then stack all treated-control sets and estimate a difference-in-difference model with

extensive fixed effects for cross sections and time periods. Web Appendix D presents an

illustrative example of the data structure, highlighting that control units are never treated while

Page 19

they serve as controls. Moreover, as we highlight in the Robustness Check section, we also

estimate an alternative two-stage approach (Gardner et al. 2024) that explicitly takes the

staggered treatment timing into account, and find very comparable results.

Second, the timing of a brand manufacturer’s deletion decision for a given market and

retailer is unlikely to be random, and competing brands may strategically employ their marketing

mix to improve the share of revenue they gain after a brand deletion. We correct for the

endogeneity of the deletion decision and marketing mix using a control function approach with

Hausman-style instruments, explained below. Third, the deletion effect may be dynamic rather

than constant over time, as it may take a few weeks or months before the deletion is complete,

which we accommodate through our continuous TreatPost variable defined earlier.

Treated and Control Units

The treated units are competing brands sold at retailers in markets where the focal brand

is transitioning from being available to being deleted. To create a comparable control unit (i.e.,

where the focal brand is not deleted yet) for each treated unit, we select the possible controls to

match the treated units. We use as a control the same competing brand as the treated competing

brand in the same time period at the same retailer, but in different markets that still feature the

(not yet) deleted brand. For example, if competing brand b at retailer r in market 1 is potentially

benefiting from the deletion of brand p, we use brand b by retailer r in markets 2, 3, and 4 as

control units if brand p is still active in these markets. By using the same brand b and retailer r,

we ensure the treated and control brands are identical in general brand characteristics (e.g.,

publicity, national brand advertising) and retailer characteristics (e.g., fit of brand with retailer

positioning, strength of retailer). By design, this implies that the market(s) in which a brand b at

retailer r is deleted last will not have control unit.

Page 20

Thus, potential control units are the same competing brand, sold at the same retailer,

operating in all markets where the focal brand still operates. To find the most similar control

units, we match based on log weekly revenue and log marketing mix in the year prior to the start

of the deletion at time T0. Matching on the pretreatment outcome (log revenue) entails matching

on unobservable brand–market characteristics that relate to the outcome measure itself (Abadie

2021), which is desirable because it means the analysis accounts for unobservables.4 For each

potential control, we calculate the correlations between the treated unit’s and potential control

unit’s weekly log revenue and five log marketing mix variables across these 52 weeks. To ensure

parallel trends pretreatment, we select for each treated unit up to 10 control units (in line with,

e.g., Bollinger and Sexton 2023, p. 292; Keller and Guyt 2025, pp. 11-12) that each must have an

average correlation of at least .8 with the treated unit across these six variables. A correlation of

.8 is typically considered high, and we note that this threshold already leads to a high average

pretreatment correlation of > .89 (Table 4) between treated and control units. However, we

acknowledge that it is an arbitrary threshold and assess the robustness of our findings to even

higher thresholds of .85 and .90, respectively (see Additional Checks section).

4 It is possible to consider other variables in defining control units. However, our approach is to define control markets as similar to the treatment market by considering how similar revealed brand preferences (revenue) and revealed marketing mix activity (marketing variables) are between markets. Underlying these similarities (e.g. preferences for budget brands) may be certain demographics (e.g., low wages), but we believe it is more direct to use observed preferences and marketing mix conduct to find control units similar to the treated unit.

Page 21

Parallel Trends

A key assumption of the difference-in-differences model is that the treated unit’s outcome

would have been the control unit’s outcome in the absence of the treatment. We cannot test the

posttreatment parallel trends assumption, because the counterfactual outcome is not observed,

but we can assess whether treated and control units evolve in parallel prior to the treatment.

Figure 4a shows visual evidence of parallel trends for revenue, with an average pretreatment

correlation of .998. Figure 4b shows the pretreatment deviation test (where we control for cross-

section and time fixed effects). For 50 [48] out of 52 weeks, there is no statistical difference

(p>.05) [p>.1], which is close to what is expected by chance.5 We also conduct an in-time

placebo test, where we set the treatment date 26 weeks before the actual treatment. The

difference is negligible (b = -.001, p=.837), confirming pretreatment parallel trends.

Table 5 shows that revenue changes notably for all brand types. After the deletion, all

three brand types gain sales, at between 1.19% and 1.57% of their before-deletion levels. In

terms of marketing variables, we find that while promotion prices hardly change, feature

advertising, regular price, line length, and distribution generally increase following the deletion.

Noting the usual caveats regarding model-free comparisons, we turn to our formal analysis to

provide cleaner estimates of brand deletion effects.

Difference-in-Differences Model for Brand Revenue

As discussed, the treatment and control pairs meet the pretreatment parallel-trends

assumption. Following Li and Van den Bulte (2023, p. 751), “if the testable part of the DID

parallel trends assumption holds, then use the DID method,” we adopt a moderated difference-in-

differences model. We stack weekly observations for all treated units and all control units (up to

10 per treated unit), for a total of 55,876,309 observations across all market-retailer-category-

Page 23

brand-week combinations. We estimate a moderated difference-in-differences model for the

effect of brand deletion on competing brand revenue, accounting for moderators, marketing mix

effects and changes therein, control variables, and endogeneity control functions:

Identification Challenges

The treated versus control unit approach accounts for unobservables that could drive the

revenue change, but we note other potential threats to identification that require attention,

including the timing of the brand deletion and the endogenous nature of marketing mix tools.

Endogeneity of the timing of brand deletion

The order in which a brand manufacturer deletes a brand from different markets and

retailers may not be random but instead could be determined by the strength of the remaining

sister brands in these markets or other unobserved factors. Endogenous timing of the brand

deletion would be reflected in the 𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝 variable, which starts to take on non-zero

values once the brand deletion begins. Unobserved revenue confounders may be correlated with

this variable, in which case the parameter estimates of Equation 1 may be inconsistent

(Wooldridge 2010). To address this concern, we specify a first-stage model using exogenous

variation to explain the extent to which brand p is deleted from competing brand b’s category c

in market m at retailer r in week t, as reflected in 𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝. From this model, we derive

the residual 𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶_𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝 and include it in Equation 1 to alleviate the endogeneity

equation / math rendering (image)

concern.

Page 25

To model 𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝, we include an instrumental variable. This instrument must

meet the criteria of strength, validity, and granularity (Shi, Grewal, and Sridhar 2021), i.e., it

should (1) correlate with the outcome variable (whether a brand is deleted), (2) not affect the

unobserved parts of competing brands’ revenues, and (3) vary at the same level as the data.

Following Sridhar et al. (2016) and Keller and Guyt (2023), we leverage institutional

insights to determine an appropriate instrument, namely, the share of neighbors-of-neighboring

markets in which the brand has already been deleted at the retailer. A market (DMA) has

neighboring markets, which in turn have their own neighbors, which we define as neighbors of

neighbors. For example, the Lafayette, LA, market has three neighbors (Lake Charles, LA,

Alexandria, LA, and Baton Rouge, LA). Lake Charles, LA, has one neighbor that is not a

neighbor of Lafayette, LA (Beaumont-Port Arthur), Alexandria, LA, has two (Shreveport and

Monroe-El Dorado), and Baton Rouge’s neighbors include New Orleans, LA, and Jackson, MS.

Together, these 5 markets are Lafayette’s neighbors’ neighbors. If two out of these five neighbors

have deleted the brand already, the instrument takes the value .4 (=2/5).

The rationale for the instrument is as follows. Brands are typically managed and

distributed by geographic regions covering multiple markets. The decision to delete a brand from

a region is usually made for all markets in that region, regardless of individual market

performance. Even if a single market represents a success, it may not be enough to support the

overall overhead costs of distributing and managing the entire region. Because contracts and

inventory levels vary across retailers and markets, the brand does not disappear simultaneously

but sequentially, so brand deletions in neighbors-of-neighboring markets could be informative

about whether a deletion is imminent for the focal market (leading to instrument strength; see

also Hwang, Bronnenberg, and Thomadsen (2010) and Keller and Guyt (2023)). Whether a brand

Page 26

is deleted in neighbors-of-neighboring markets (hundreds of miles away) should not affect

demand for that brand in the focal market, as consumers do not travel hundreds of miles for

grocery shopping (creating instrument validity, i.e., meeting the exclusion restriction). We focus

on neighbors’ neighbors (rather than direct neighbors) to avoid potential cross-market demand

spillovers. The share of neighbors’ neighbors where the brand has already been delisted at a

given retailer varies at the same level as our data, so this instrumental variable also meets the

granularity criterion. Finally, we note that the instrument in the first-stage regression is positively

and strongly related to the brand deletion decision (𝑏𝑏 = .513, p < .001); see Web Appendix G.

Endogeneity of the marketing mix

Brand managers may be strategic in setting their marketing mix, and those decisions can

be driven by unobserved demand shocks that vary cross-sectionally or over time. Cross-sectional

shocks reflect unobserved differences across market-retailer-brand combinations, such that a

brand may be more popular in some markets and therefore command a price premium. To

safeguard against this potential endogeneity concern, we only use within-market-retailer-

category-brand variation by including market-retailer-category-brand fixed effects 𝛼𝛼𝑏𝑏𝑏𝑏𝑏𝑏𝑏𝑏. The

unobserved brand factors could also be time-varying (see, e.g., Papies, Ebbes, and van Heerde

2017), but the quasi-experimental method and chosen control units implicitly account for time-

varying brand-specific factors’ effect on the treatment effect (e.g., national brand advertising),

because the control units pertain to the same brand at the same time.

What remains are time-varying factors specific to a given market-retailer-category-brand

pair, as when brands strategically adjust their marketing mix response locally at a given market

or retailer. To address this source of endogeneity, we use a control function approach with

Hausman-style instruments. For example, for regular price, the instrumental variable is the

Page 27

average regular price of the same brand b at the same retailer in neighbors’ neighboring markets

in the same week. In the first stage, we regress all marketing mix variables on the instrumental

variables and control variables, and include the residuals (𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶_𝑀𝑀𝑀𝑀𝑀𝑀𝑀𝑀𝑘𝑘,𝑏𝑏𝑏𝑏𝑏𝑏𝑏𝑏𝑏𝑏) in Equation 1.

The rationale for instrument relevance for regular price is that underlying cost factors for

ingredients, packaging, transportation, and labor may exhibit regional and longitudinal variation,

affecting regular prices both in the focal market and its neighbors’ neighbors (see also Ma et al.

(2011) and Keller and Guyt (2023)). The identifying assumption is that markets operate in

comparable economic environments and face similar cost shocks (e.g., due to price fluctuations

or transportation costs), which influence marketing mix decisions. Thus, changes in the

marketing mix at the same retailer in markets that are neighbors’ neighbors should correlate with

changes in the marketing mix for the retailer in focal markets, implying that the instrument is

relevant and strong. Indeed, we find that the instruments in the first-stage regressions are all

positively related to the endogenous variables (parameters range from .722 to .942, all p < .001),

attesting to the instruments’ strength. Multivariate Sanderson-Windmeijer tests also attest to the

strength of each instrument (all p < .001); see Web Appendix G for details.

To satisfy the exclusion restriction, no common demand shocks should affect both

markets, which is why we use neighbors’ neighbors markets, as before. Because we aggregate

across all neighbors’ neighboring markets, it is unlikely that the instrument is affected by market-

level idiosyncratic shocks (Sridhar et al. 2016). Therefore, we argue that the instruments are

valid and satisfy the exclusion restriction. Finally, instruments need to exhibit sufficient

granularity (Shi et al. 2021). In our case, they do; the average marketing mix across neighbors’

neighboring markets in a given week varies at the same level (across markets, retailers,

Page 28

categories, brands, and time) as our focal marketing mix variable.7

We estimate Equation 1 (and 2 below) with OLS using clustered errors at the retailer-

category-brand level to account for potential autocorrelation and correlation across markets.

Following Papies et al. (2017), we adjust the standard errors to reflect that the control function

terms are estimated quantities.

revenue. Stacking the same observations (where the same treated units are paired with the same

up to 10 control units), we now estimate a difference-in-differences model for each marketing

variable (k=1,…,5) separately:

RESULTS

Difference-in-Differences Model Results for Brand Revenue

To understand the effect of brand deletion on competing brand revenue, we turn to the

corresponding difference-in-differences model (Equation 1), the results of which are in Table 6.

The model fits the data well (R2 = .848) and collinearity does not appear to be an issue, as also

confirmed in Web Appendix J, where we incrementally add blocks of variables to the model,

starting with just intercept shifts. Web Appendix C also provides a correlation matrix among the

key variables. Most of the control function terms are significant at the 10% level, indicating the

relevance of accounting for the endogeneity of marketing conduct and the delisting decision. We

do note that Web Appendix J shows that directionally, the findings are not different when we

leave out the control function terms.

Results for Brand Deletion Effects on Competing Brand Revenues

Table 6 shows that the effect of brand deletion is generally positive, but not significant

for rival national brands (b=.004; p=.661) and sister brands (b=.009; p=.588), while private

labels gain revenue (b=.021, p=.035)9. These effects hold for moderators and marketing mix kept

at their means, as all covariates are mean-centered. However, as discussed below in Table 9,

8 In an auxiliary analysis, we also measure the impact of a brand deletion on whether retailers launch new brands in the category. Specifically, we assess whether the rate of new brands (measured in three ways: brands (i) new to the market-retailer pair, (ii) new to the market, and (iii) new to the category) differs between market-retailer-category combinations with a brand deletion versus its control markets. Using a difference-in-difference specification, we find that the rate of launching new brands is not different depending on whether a brand deletion takes place or not. Table 6. Effect of Brand Deletion, Moderators, Marketing Mix on Competitor Revenue

Table 6 shows that competing brands gain more revenue when they are more similarly

priced to the deleted brand (b=.028, p=.010), indicating consumers may switch to similarly-

Page 31

priced competitors rather than brands with a different price positioning. Competing brands also

gain when the deleted brand had a higher market share (b=.246, p<.001), which makes sense as

there is more demand to redistribute. A higher category concentration limits the gain for

competing brands (b=-.158, p<.001), as consumers may find it harder to find a substitute in a

category with fewer yet bigger brands. The market share of the competitor has a marginally

significant effect on revenue (b=.034, p=.106), indicating that larger brands may be better

positioned to scoop up revenue from the deleted brand. The category growth does not materially

affect the revenue of competing brands.

Results for Marketing Mix Effectiveness

Both the dependent variable and the marketing mix covariates are in log form, and the

parameters can be interpreted as elasticities with respect to revenue. The parameter estimates for

the marketing mix are face valid. The promotional price elasticities (stronger in magnitude than

regular price elasticities, as expected; Bijmolt, van Heerde, and Pieters 2005) are negative for

rival national brands (b=-1.765, p<.001), sister brands (b=-1.685, p<.001), and for private labels

(b=-1.591, p<.001). The parameter for feature advertising is also an elasticity (percentage change

in revenue due to a 1% increase in feature support), as feature support is defined as the log of the

weighted fraction of stores and products having feature advertising for the brand in that week.

Feature advertising has positive yet weak elasticities on brand revenue for all types of brands:

rival national brands (b=.034, p< .001), sister brands (b=.037, p<.001), and for private labels

(b=.021, p<.001). Regular price elasticities for brand revenue are negative for rival national

brands (b=-.049, p=.046), sister brands (b=-.256, p=.014), and for private labels (b=-.179,

p<.001), suggesting price-elastic brand demand in unit sales. Line length elasticities are positive

and strong in magnitude for rival national brands (b=1.266, p<.001), sister brands (b=1.325,

Page 32

p<.001), and (at a lower magnitude) for private labels (b=1.190, p<.001).10 We find very strong

positive distribution elasticities for rival national brands (b=2.942, p<.001), sister brands

(b=3.098, p<.001), and for private labels (b=3.586, p<.001). We note that these distribution

elasticities are based on within-retailer, within-market time series variation and therefore not

directly comparable to more aggregate distribution elasticities based on national-level time series

variation.11

Results for Brand Deletion Effect on Competitor Marketing Conduct

We now discuss competing brands’ marketing mix changes after a brand deletion.12 Table

7 shows the results from Equation 2. Focusing on the focal treatment x post parameters, i.e., the

relative change in marketing conduct of the treated markets to the control markets, we find that

(for moderators at their means) rival national brands offer slightly deeper promotion price

discounts (b=-.001, p=.043), as do competing brands that are larger (b=-.002, p=.001), possibly

indicating more sizeable resources to react. Store brands offer deeper promotions if private labels

are present (b=-.003, p=.007), as do private labels, if store brands are present (b=-.001, p=.003).

These findings suggest that, especially when store brands and private labels are both present,

they strongly compete through price promotion in the wake of the brand deletion.

Conversely, price promotions are shallower for brands that have lower price similarity to

10 In a robustness check, we also added a brand’s fraction of SKUs that are new to the category since the beginning of the brand deletion as an additional moderator (interacted with TreatPost and Post). The interaction effect with TreatPost is economically small (b=.043, p=.386) while the focal parameters are not affected in sign or magnitude. We present these results in Web Appendix K. 11 Web Appendix L discusses the magnitude of the distribution elasticities in more depth, including a transformation to (much lower) national distribution elasticities. 12 We report on the change relative to the brand’s control markets (𝛽𝛽𝑘𝑘,𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐). We could also consider the overall (before-after) change accounting for the control group’s change (𝛿𝛿𝑘𝑘,𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐), i.e., 𝛽𝛽𝑘𝑘,𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐+ 𝛿𝛿𝑘𝑘,𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐. For rival national brands, the overall promotion intensity shows no change (-.0006 + .0004 = -.0002, p=.572), while it becomes shallower for sister brands (i.e., at the same rate as the control group; .0017, p=.047). Rival national brand’s feature advertising decreases at a lower rate than in the control group (-.0528, p<.001). Finally, line length decreases for rival national brands at the same rate as control units (-.0111, p=.003) and line length increases at the same rate as control units for private labels (.0132, p=.011).

the deleted brand (b=.001, p<.001), possibly reflecting that the deleted brand served customers in

a different price segment. Price promotions are also shallower the larger the deleted brand was

(b=.005, p=.012), reflecting reduced competitive pressure.

Relative to control markets, rival national brands (b=.022, p=.013) increase feature

Page 34

advertising after a brand deletion. Private labels do so too (b=.048, p<.001), but only if there is

no sister brand present (b=-.049, p=.013). Sister brands only increase their feature advertising if

a private label is present (b=.058, p=.015). We find that competing brands especially increase

feature advertising when the deleted brand’s market share is higher (b=.239, p<.001).

We find all brand types to increase their regular price relative to control markets: +2.38%

for rival national brands (b=.024, p<.001), +3.40% for sister brands (b=.033, p<.001), and

+1.20% for private labels (b=.012, p<.001). Results for the moderators show that regular price

changes are larger when the deleted brand had a higher market share (b=.030, p=.042), which is

indicative of changes in the competitive structure as removing larger brands reduces competitive

pressure more. Regular price changes are smaller when the competitor’s price more closely

matched the deleted brand’s (b=-.005, p=.058). For private labels, regular price rises more if a

sister brand is present (b=.009, p=.075); conversely, prices rise less for sister brands if private

labels are present (b=-.007, p=.051).

On average, line length remains – compared to the control units – stable across all brand

types. However, rival national brands’ line length is reduced if private labels are present (b=-

.007, p<.001), reflective of retailers trying to keep national brand power in check. Line length

increases when the competing brand has a higher market share to start with (b=.015, p=.045) or

the category is more concentrated (b=.019, p=.009); indicative of brands’ greater power.

However, line length declines when the deleted brand had a higher market share (b=-.160,

p<.001), indicative of softened competition. Also, line length is reduced when the competing

brand is priced more similarly (b=-.007, p=.016), possibly because a comparable brand continues

to exist.

In response to the focal brand’s deletion, all brand types increase their distribution: rival

Page 35

national brand (b=.006, p<.001), sister brands (b=.011, p=.012), and private labels (b=.006,

p<.001). However, private labels only do so if no sister brand is present (b=-.005, p=.079), and

sister brands (b=-.009, p=.055) and rival national brands (b=-.002, p=.054) only do so if no

private label is present. The moderator findings further show that lower distribution increases

with higher category concentration (b=-.012, p=.057). Collectively, this hints at a hierarchy

where retailers aim to first increase distribution of their private labels, followed by sister brands,

which may have had more time to push for increased distribution compared to other competitors.

Net Revenue Effect

To establish the economic significance of marketing mix adjustments after a brand

deletion, we calculate the additional revenue these adjustments generate compared to the

baseline revenue change brands would experience without any marketing adjustments. To take

the brand-type specific moderator values into account, we calculate the baseline effect, which is

Table 9 shows that the marketing conduct impact in the wake of a brand deletion is

substantial. For sister brands, the observed increase in distribution adds 1.83% to revenue, while

the line length adds .84%, which helps to boost the smaller baseline effect of .51%, leading to an

overall revenue gain of 2.77% due to the brand deletion. Rival national brands manage to

roughly double their baseline gain (+.74%) through marketing conduct (+.63%) to a total

revenue gain of 1.36%, primarily through a distribution gain (+1.23%). Starting with a

substantial baseline effect of +2.28%, some of the marketing conduct by private labels helps

them (distribution increase adds 1.77%; feature advertising .09%), but other marketing conduct

hurts: regular price hike reduces revenue by -.25%, line length reduction lowers revenue by -

.45%. Still, private labels gain 3.45% in revenue in the wake of the brand deletion.

Considering the sizable marketing impact results in Table 9, we conclude that competing

brands have considerable leverage to sway revenue gains their way through their marketing

conduct after a brand deletion.

Net Revenue Implications for Brand Manufacturers

Using the net revenue effects for each competing brand (see Table 9), we assess how

much sister brands gain after a brand deletion. For the manufacturer of both the sister brand and

the deleted brand, the key question is whether the sister brand’s gain covers a substantial share of

the deleted brand’s former revenue. In other words, can manufacturers succeed in “killing a

brand, keeping a customer” (Kumar 2003, p. 86)? Although manufacturers may attempt to

persuade customers to switch to sister brands in their brand portfolio, sister brands typically are

positioned to minimize overlap and target distinct customer segments. Thus, customers are

unlikely to view a sister brand as the most suitable alternative. Moreover, deleting a brand may

create knowledge gaps for the manufacturer about how to serve customers.

Page 38

To assess how a manufacturer’s category revenues change when it deletes a brand, we

calculate the cumulative revenue change across all remaining sister brands in the category for

each market-retailer pair and compare it to the deleted brand’s pretreatment revenue. The

difference reveals the net revenue effect for the manufacturer. If the change is equivalent to the

deleted brand’s revenue, it retains 100%; if the revenue change for sister brands is smaller

(larger), it retains less (more) than 100%. We then aggregate these results across all market-

retailer pairs with at least one sister brand (on average, 1.36 sister brands were active).

For example, Wisk, a Sun Products brand that was deleted from the “Detergents - Heavy

Duty – Liquid” category, earned $7.13M in annual national revenues in this category in our

sample (conditional on a sister brand being present). After deletion, its Sun Products–owned

sister brands gained $2.04M (on average, Wisk had with 3.79 sister brands), leading to a net

revenue loss of -$5.09M (=$2.04M–$7.13M). Thus, the manufacturer recouped 28.52% (=

[2.04/7.13]×100%) of the deleted brand’s revenues through its sister brands. As Web Appendix

M shows, across the 215 deleted brands with sister brands, manufacturers recoup on average

37.76% of deleted-brand revenue (the average deleted brand earned $485,799 per year per

market-retailer pair, and sister brands recouped $183,453), though variation is substantial.

Results for Effect of Brand Deletion on Category Revenue

Table 10 reports on Equation 3, showing that the category revenue reduces by a net 2.3%

(b=-.024, p<.001) in the wake of the focal brand’s deletion. The model controls for the revenue

effects of category-level regular price (b=.597, p<.001), feature advertising (b=.077, p<.001),

and line length (b=.682, p<.001).

We conduct several robustness checks to establish the sensitivity of our findings to

modeling decisions. We describe these robustness checks in greater detail in Web Appendix N,

where we also present detailed parameter estimates for the revenue model.

As a first robustness check, we assess the sensitivity of our revenue model results to the

beginning of the brand deletion, which is determined using a moving average, by setting set T0

(the beginning of the deletion) to two weeks before the week in our focal analyses and re-

estimating our models. Second, we account for the staggered timing of treatment by employing a

stacked DID approach. By carefully selecting control units that are never treated within the

treated unit’s timeframe, it avoids the bias that can arise in standard two-way fixed effects

models, which mix valid and invalid comparisons (i.e., later-vs-earlier treated) when treatments

are heterogeneous (Baker, Larcker, and Wang 2022; Goodman-Bacon 2021). As a robustness

check, we apply a two-stage DID approach (Gardner et al. 2024) that accounts for staggered

adoption. In the first stage, we remove group and time patterns using untreated observations to

create adjusted outcomes; in the second stage, we estimate treatment effects on these adjusted

values. This design eliminates problematic later-vs-earlier contrasts. Third, we construct

counterfactuals for each treated brand using highly correlated control units. Our main analysis

Page 40

requires an average correlation of 𝜌𝜌̅ > .80 revenue and marketing mix trajectories for the treated

and control brands, ensuring close comparability. In two robustness checks, we use higher

minimum average correlations of 𝜌𝜌̅ > .85 and 𝜌𝜌̅ > .90. Fourth, while our focal model uses

clustered errors at the retailer-category-deleted brand-competing brand level, we also implement

clustered standard errors at the panel (i.e., market-retailer-category-deleted brand-competing

brand) level as an alternative to account for autocorrelation only.

Fifth, we assess to what extent our results in the revenue model are driven by the

corrections for endogeneity. To this end, we estimate three additional versions of Equation 1:

without any control-function terms, with only the control-function term for the deletion decision,

and with only control-function terms for the marketing mix. Sixth, because brand deletions occur

at different times across markets and retailers, we exploit this staggered timing by using not-yet-

deleted cases as controls. To test whether timing matters, we compare early versus late deletions.

A relevant question is whether effects differ between early versus late brand deletion cases. To

investigate, we divide the sample into “Early deletion” cases (start date before the median) and

“Late deletion” cases (after the median) and add an interaction effect of treatment x post with an

indicator for Early deletion (base = Late deletion) in Equation 1. Seventh, it is conceivable that

the five marketing mix variables have interactive effects and that there are decreasing returns to

scale for line length. We added all 10 pairwise interactions to Equation 1, and separately added

the squared log line length.

We find the parameter estimates to be very similar to the focal estimates, with an average

correlation of .990 across robustness checks. We also note that the average proportion of

estimates that are different in terms of significance (i.e., p-value just below vs. above .1)

compared to the focal estimates (.06) is less than would be expected by chance (.1).

Page 41

DISCUSSION

Brand manufacturers regularly prune their brand portfolios by deleting brands from a

given product category. Despite the prevalence of brand deletions, their consequences are not

well understood. We therefore adopt an empirics-first approach and assess – based on 1,046

brand deletions across 384 categories affecting 63k market-retailer-category-brand combinations

– the effect of a brand’s deletion on competing brands that remain active in the category. In so

doing, we answer the four research questions introduced at the start.

First, we assess whether rival national brands, sister national brands, or private labels

benefit from a brand’s deletion. We find that – absent the impact of moderators and marketing

conduct – rival national brands and sister brands experience no loss or gain, while private labels

gain revenue in the wake of the brand deletion (Table 6; path A in Figure 1). When we add the

impact of the moderators (research question 2; Table 9; path B in Figure 1), the revenue effect

turns positive for all competing brands: rival national brands (+1.36%), sister brands (+2.77%),

and private labels (+3.45%), for an average of +1.73%. The findings for the moderators add

nuance to these insights, showing that competing brands gain more revenue when the competing

brand had higher price similarity with the deleted brand, when the deleted brand’s pre-deletion

market share is higher, and when the category is less concentrated.

Further nuance is added by considering research question 3 about the extent to which

competing brands change their marketing conduct after a brand deletion (path C in Figure 1).

After accounting for the impact of moderators on marketing conduct (path D in Figure 1), we

find that all brand types increase their regular price. However, because their price elasticity of

revenue is negative, they experience a drop in revenue due to this move. All brand types manage

to increase their distribution in the wake of the brand deletion, which, when combined with

strong distribution elasticities, leads to reasonably sizeable revenue gains of 1.23%-1.83% due to

Page 42

this form of marketing conduct across the three brand types. One surprising result is that only

sister brands increase their line length in the wake of the brand deletion (Table 8), which

(combined with a strong line length elasticity) generates an additional .84% revenue gain. A

plausible explanation is that sister brands may have access to brand deletion information earlier,

enabling them to plan line extensions in advance and thus react more quickly, preempting line

extensions by others. In addition, they may benefit from reallocated resources, as the budget

from the deleted brand can be used to support line length expansion.

Combining these insights allows us to address the final research question, which is how

competing brands fare overall after the brand deletion, taking into account the extent to which

they engage in marketing conduct changes (Table 9). We find that overall, private labels benefit

the most (+3.45% revenue), with sister brands in second place (+2.77%) and rival national

brands in third (+1.36%). Given that the vast majority of competing brands (80%) are rival

national brands, the overall average revenue gain is 1.73%. We do note there is a lot of

heterogeneity underlying these findings and a big role for marketing conduct, discussed next.

Marketing Conduct Insights

We document new insights with respect to brands’ marketing conduct (relative to the

control group) in the wake of a brand deletion, which we summarize in Table 11. We document

four types of patterns. One pattern is a lost opportunity where marketing effectiveness is strong,

but the marketing conduct change is minor, which we observe for price promotion for all brand

types. A second pattern is spoiled arms, where marketing conduct change is in the right direction,

but the effectiveness is weak, with feature advertising as a prime example, especially for private

labels. A third pattern is a seized opportunity, where marketing conduct is adjusted in the right

direction and the effectiveness is strong. The lift in distribution is a prime example for all three

Page 43

brand types, as is the lift in line length for sister brands. The final and worst pattern is a self-

inflicted loss, where an effective marketing variable is adjusted in the opposite direction from

what would benefit revenue. The regular price hikes across all competitor brand types is one

example of a self-inflicted loss, as are line length cuts by rival national brands and private labels.

Table 11. Insights on How Competing Brands Can Capitalize on Brand Deletions

Page 44

Managerial Implications

Marketing literature is replete with advice on how to build brands (e.g., Ataman, Mela,

and van Heerde 2008). In contrast, there is relatively little advice about how to deal with brand

deletions. Doing nothing is a reasonable course of action for private labels (revenue +2.28%), but

much less successful for rival national brands (+.74%) and particularly sister brands (+.51%). We

recommend a more active response, and we highlight the promise of active marketing conduct,

designed to capitalize on the opportunity created by a brand deletion (see also Table 9). One

obvious caveat to the managerial implications presented next is that rival and sister brands may

have different degrees of agency over marketing decisions. That is, while promotion price and

feature advertising are primarily manufacturer-driven, regular price and line length are co-

decided with retailers, while distribution is governed by retailers. We also note that our

recommendations focus on revenue (rather than profit) implications of marketing conduct, as we

lack data on the cost of changes in marketing and on profit margins.

Rival national brands

For rival national brands, deploying price promotion is a feasible, effective, yet

underutilized form of marketing conduct in the wake of a brand deletion (see Table 11). Even if

price promotions might threaten to undermine a premium brand image or brand equity in the

long term (Jedidi, Mela, and Gupta 1999), they can strongly boost brand revenue in the short

term to seize customers from the deleted brand. Feature advertising, in contrast, does not

necessarily need to be increased given its relatively weak effectiveness.

When rival national brands decide with retailers on regular price in the wake of the brand

deletion, one important input into this decision is the relatively inelastic price response (-.049) of

the revenue of rival national brands. In a way, the inelastic response justifies the fairly strong

Page 45

regular price rise we document for these brands (+2.44%). As for line length, rival national

brands should point out to retailers that the strong line length elasticities (around 1.3) warrant

extending the brand’s line length carried by the retailer, which is opposite to the shrinkage (-

.50%) that we document empirically. To convince retailers to carry the brand in more stores, rival

national brand manufacturers should point out the strong distribution elasticity (2.942).

Sister brands

The recommendations for sister brands are largely parallel to those for rival national

brands. They should also offer more price promotions (without a need for feature advertising)

and point to strong line length and distribution elasticities to convince retailers to carry their

SKUs in more stores. One diverging implication emerges for regular price: given the relatively

strong elasticity of revenue to regular price for sister brands (-.256), the observed strong increase

in regular price (+2.90%) caused self-inflicted revenue losses. Mitigating regular price increases

(or even reducing regular price after a brand deletion) is recommended for sister brands.

Looking at the bigger picture, for manufacturers that maintain multiple brands in a

category and plan to delete one, our findings provide cold comfort. Sister brands recoup less than

40% of the revenue lost due to the brand deletion on average. Of course, other considerations

(unobservable to us) might prompt manufacturers to delete a brand from a category (e.g.,

efficiency gains in brand management, supply issues), but from an overall revenue perspective,

we suggest caution.

Private labels

Our findings are especially encouraging for private labels. Private labels gain, on

average, 2.28% revenue from a brand deletion if they keep their marketing mix unchanged.

Moreover, private labels have full control over all marketing variables as these brands are owned

Page 46

by retailers. Capitalizing on their strong distribution elasticity (3.586), private labels should

increase their distribution (if it is not at 100% yet), seizing the shelf space left vacant by the

deleted brand. Private labels’ second and third strongest elasticities are for price promotion (-

1.591) and line length (1.190), making price promotion and line length extension effective (yet

currently underutilized) ways to attract customers in the wake of the brand deletion. Given

feature advertising’s relatively weak elasticity (.021), we again suggest caution. Although feature

advertising is relatively easy to deploy as a marketing tactic (and private labels eagerly do so),

we find it is not an effective way to gain revenue after brand deletion.

Overall, while private label marketing effectiveness is somewhat weaker on average than

sister brands and rival national brands (except for distribution, where they dominate national

brands), they can gain a lot of ground by making judicious adjustments to their most powerful

marketing variables, such as distribution, price promotion, and line length. Thus, while an

inactive stance in response to a brand deletion will bring some benefits to private labels, an

active stance (i.e., increasing marketing support to capitalize on the deletion) can potentially

produce strong payoffs.

Limitations and Further Research

While we shed some first light on the consequences of brand deletions, we suggest that

follow-up research could investigate their antecedents (which is beyond the scope of this study).

A variety of possible motives might drive manufacturers to delete brands from the market,

including economic (lack of profitability), branding (creating opportunities for sister brand

growth), supply (difficulty of sourcing inputs), knowledge (lack of in-firm category expertise), or

brand consistency (deleted brand does not fit the rest of the brand portfolio) motives.

Investigating the prevalence and strength of these different motives for brand deletions can shed

Page 47

additional light on this under-researched domain. The decision to delete a brand has potentially

many antecedents, some of which are observable (e.g., the presence of sister brands) but others

are unobservable (change in focus, anticipation of competitors).

Unfortunately, we lack advertising data for all markets, retailers, categories, brands, and

time periods. However, recent research studying U.S. grocery products reports very small

advertising elasticities (.0098-.0261; Shapiro, Hitsch, and Tuchman 2021), suggesting minimal

advertising effects. We also note that national advertising influences both treated and control

units, so even with such data, isolating a treatment effect would not be feasible.

Furthermore, we document the revenue consequences of brand deletions using retail

scanner data, highlighting a promising avenue for examining how brand pruning affects investor

and firm value. In the introduction, we reference large-scale pruning initiatives by firms such as

P&G (100 brands deleted) and Coca-Cola (200 brands). Future research could investigate how

these strategies influence firm value (e.g., abnormal returns or Tobin’s Q). Such research could

quantify both the magnitude and mechanisms of these effects – for instance, whether cost savings

offset potential revenue losses.

Our sample frame covers each market’s top 10 competing brands and each market’s top 3

retailers to ensure enough economic substance. Given this decision rule, we had to omit smaller

competing brands that are not among the 10 leading competing brands in the market, but may be

a top 10 competing brand within a given retailer.

In summary, we believe this study makes some meaningful headway in understanding the

consequences of brand deletions and how competing brands can seize the opportunities by

engaging with their marketing mix. We further hope this study stimulates new research into this

important yet underexplored marketing domain.

Web Appendix D: Illustrative Data Structure of Treated and Control Cases

In this illustrative example, we consider the deletion of brand D by retailer R in markets M1 and M2. Brand D is deleted in market M1 (M2) in week 53 (183). Market M2 serves as control unit for market M1; market M3 (to be deleted even later) serves as control unit for market M2. The data structure shows that while M2 serves as control unit (weeks 1 – 105), it is “never treated”. Table W2 and Figure W2 illustrate the data structure.

Web Appendix H: Category Revenue Model

To assess the category revenue implications of a brand deletion, we aggregate the data

from all 14,462 market-retailer-category-deleted brand combinations across competing brands to

the market-retailer-category-week level. Irrespective of whether brands meet the sample criteria

in our focal analysis, revenue and line length are the sum across all competing brands, category

price is value sales divided by volume sales, and feature advertising is the average share of SKUs

(by brand) that is being featured in a given week.

We perform the same aggregation for all potential control units (market-retailer-category

combinations where the deleted brand was still active in) and calculate the average pre-deletion

correlation between each treated and potential control case for the four outcome variables

(revenue, category price, category feature advertising, and category line length). We retain the

ten control cases with the highest pre-deletion correlation as long as it is > .8, as in the focal

analysis. This leads to 6,144 treated cases at the category-market-retailer level with 3.5 control

cases on average (N = 3,490,503); thus, the set of treated and control cases does not fully overlap

with the analyses at the brand level.

We estimate a similar control function for the endogeneity of the TreatPost term with the

same instrument. The instrument is positively and significantly related to the TreatPost variable

(b = .573, SE = .007, p < .001).
