Web Appendix N: Robustness Checks

We conduct several robustness checks to establish the sensitivity of our findings to modeling

decisions, which we describe in more detail below. We report the results in Table WA5 of this Web

Appendix.

First, we empirically determine the beginning of a brand’s deletion using changes in the

(moving-average) distribution as noted in the “Data and Measures” section. As we are using a moving

average, the brand deletion may have started earlier than detected by our decision rule. To assess this

possibility, we set T0 (the beginning of the deletion) to two weeks before the week in our focal analyses

and re-estimate our models.

Second, we leverage a staggered adoption setting with a stacked DID approach. In the presence

of heterogeneous effects, a standard two-way fixed effects (TWFE) regression coefficient may lead to

biased treatment effect estimates (Baker, Larcker, and Wang 2022; Goodman-Bacon 2021). In that case,

the standard TWFE regression does not offer a single clean DID estimate, but a weighted average of

three types of comparisons: (i) treated versus never-treated, (ii) early-treated versus later-treated (while

later is not yet treated), and (iii) later-treated versus earlier-treated (while earlier is already treated),

arising because TWFE mechanically uses all timing variation as identifying variation. While contrasts

(i) and (ii) are proper identification sources, source (iii) (later-vs-earlier contrasts) is problematic: it

compares newly-treated groups to already-treated groups, which are no longer valid controls when

treatment effects are heterogeneous. As detailed in the Method section, we address this issue by using

as controls only cases that are never treated within the time of the treated case. By construction, this

removes later-vs-earlier contrasts, resolving the issue.

As an alternative, we adopt a novel and computationally efficient two-stage DID estimation

approach as a robustness check (Gardner et al. 2024). The overarching idea is to first remove

underlying group and time patterns using untreated observations and then estimate treatment effects by

Page 75

W24

comparing treated outcomes to these adjusted baselines, thereby recovering an interpretable average

effect even when adoption is staggered and effects vary across groups and periods. Because earlier-

treated units (part of later-vs-earlier contrasts) never inform the baselines, source (iii) (later-vs-earlier)

contrasts disappear. Specifically, we first regress the outcome variable (revenue) on cross-section and

time fixed effects, the marketing mix, and moderators based on untreated data. We then subtract these

fixed effects from the outcome variable to obtain an adjusted outcome. In a second step, we regress the

adjusted outcome on a treatment indicator and its interaction effects with the moderator variables.

While this procedure does not deliver marketing mix effectiveness estimates based on the full sample,

it isolates the treatment effect in a way that remains valid in the presence of treatment effect

heterogeneity.

Third, we use controls to create a counterfactual for each brand’s evolution. While we imposed

a minimum average correlation of 𝜌𝜌̅ > .80 between revenue and marketing mix trajectories for the

treated and control brands (see Table 4), we also investigated whether imposing higher minimum

average correlations of 𝜌𝜌̅ > .85 or 𝜌𝜌̅ > .90 makes a difference. Using these higher thresholds reduces the

number of treatment-control pairs because there are fewer pairs meeting these thresholds, from N =

55,876,309 for our default minimum 𝜌𝜌̅ > .80, to N = 43,855,533 for 𝜌𝜌̅ > .85 and N = 28,157,212 for 𝜌𝜌̅ >

.90.

Fourth, while our focal model uses clustered errors at the retailer-category-deleted brand-

competing brand level, we also implement clustered standard errors at the panel (i.e., market-retailer-

category-deleted brand-competing brand) level as an alternative to account for autocorrelation only.

Fifth, we assess to what extent our results in the revenue model are driven by the corrections for

endogeneity. To this end, we estimate three additional versions of Equation 1: without any control-

function terms, with only the control-function term for the deletion decision, and with only control-

Page 76

W25

function terms for the marketing mix.

Sixth, a brand deletion is typically staggered across markets and retailers over months or even

years. Our difference-in-differences approach capitalizes on the spread-out nature of brand deletions by

using market-retailer-category combinations where the brand has not been deleted yet as controls for

cases where the brand deletion has already taken place. Consequently, cases where the brand deletion

occurs last lack valid controls and are excluded from the analysis. However, a relevant question is

whether effects differ between early versus late brand deletion cases. To investigate, we divide the

sample into “Early deletion” cases (start date before the median) and “Late deletion” cases (after the

median). We note that the average number of controls for the “Early deletion” group (6.12) closely

matches that for the “Late deletion” group (5.96), with no significant differences. Similarly, the average

pretreatment-control correlation for the Early deletion group (.896) does not materially differ (p=.144)

from the Late deletion group (.893). We also add an interaction effect of treatment x post with an

indicator for Early deletion (base = Late deletion) in Equation 1. We find that the added term does not

have a significant effect (b=-.000, p=.949), suggesting that the Early deletion group does not benefit

differentially from the brand deletion than the Late deletion group. The focal parameter estimates are

not affected.

Seventh, it is conceivable that the five marketing mix variables have interactive effects and that

there are decreasing returns to scale for line length. We added all 10 pairwise interactions to Equation

1, and separately added squared log line length, as reported in Table WA5. While several of these

additional terms are significant, the focal estimates preserve their sign and significance. For parsimony

reasons, we stick to the focal model.
